```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_torch <- torch::torch_is_installed()
```

```{r setup}
library(graphlearnR)
```

Graphs change. Messages are sent, payments are made, sensors report every
few minutes. graphlearnR supports three views of time, and each comes with a
rule that keeps the future out of the past.

| view | object | leakage rule |
|---|---|---|
| events in continuous time | `temporal_graph_data` | a query at time $t$ uses events with time $< t$ |
| discrete snapshots | `snapshot_sequence` | snapshot $k$ covers $[b_k, b_{k+1})$; evaluation steps come after training steps |
| signals on a fixed graph | `spatiotemporal_signal` | train, validation, and test windows are consecutive in time |

## Event graphs

A temporal graph is a stream of timestamped edges, sorted by time on
creation. `event_id` remembers the input order.

```{r}
tg <- temporal_graph_data(src = c(3, 1, 2, 1), dst = c(1, 2, 3, 3), t = c(5, 1, 3, 7),
                          edge_attr = matrix(c(0.5, 0.1, 0.3, 0.9), ncol = 1))
tg
data.frame(src = tg$src, dst = tg$dst, t = tg$t, event_id = tg$event_id)
```

### Windows and splits

`temporal_window()` keeps events with `start <= t < end`. `split_temporal()`
cuts the stream at two times, so every validation event is later than every
training event and every test event is later still.

```{r}
events <- dataset_synthetic_temporal(num_nodes = 30, num_events = 600, seed = 1)
events
sp <- split_temporal(events, val_time = 60, test_time = 80)
c(train = length(sp$train$t), val = length(sp$val$t), test = length(sp$test$t))
c(max(sp$train$t), min(sp$val$t), max(sp$val$t), min(sp$test$t))
```

### Causal neighborhoods

`temporal_neighbors()` returns the `k` most recent events of each query node
strictly before its query time. With `strict = FALSE` it also keeps events
at exactly the query time; use that only when an event at time $t$ really is
known at time $t$.

```{r}
nb <- temporal_neighbors(events, nodes = c(1, 2), times = c(50, 50), k = 3,
                         direction = "both")
nb
all(nb$t < 50)
```

## Snapshots

`temporal_snapshots()` bins events into graphs. Each snapshot uses the
half open interval $[b_k, b_{k+1})$; repeated events between the same pair
become the edge weight. With `cumulative = TRUE` snapshot $k$ holds every
event before $b_{k+1}$.

```{r}
snaps <- temporal_snapshots(events, breaks = 8)
snaps
vapply(snaps$graphs, num_edges, integer(1))
round(snaps$start, 1)
```

### Dynamic link prediction

`train_dynamic_link_model()` runs a graph GRU over the snapshots. At each
training step it predicts the edges of the *next* snapshot from everything
up to the current one, with fresh negatives. Evaluation steps are strictly
later than all training steps, and the result carries a baseline that scores
a pair by how often it appeared before.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
library(torch)
torch_manual_seed(1)
fit <- train_dynamic_link_model(snaps, hidden_dim = 16, epochs = 30, seed = 1)
fit
fit$train_steps
fit$eval_steps
fit$step_metrics
rbind(model = fit$test_metrics, history_baseline = fit$baseline_metrics)
```

Report the model next to the baseline. On many real dynamic graphs, simply
predicting that past edges repeat is hard to beat, and a model that does not
beat it has not learned anything new.

## Spatiotemporal signals

A spatiotemporal signal is a fixed graph (a road network, a sensor grid) with
a feature array of shape time by nodes by features.

```{r}
sig <- dataset_synthetic_signal(num_nodes = 15, num_steps = 80, seed = 2)
sig
dim(sig$features)
```

`train_spatiotemporal_model()` forecasts `horizon` steps ahead from `lags`
past steps with a graph GRU. Windows are assigned to training, validation,
and test sets in time order, and the naive forecast (the last observed
value) is reported next to the model.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
torch_manual_seed(2)
fst <- train_spatiotemporal_model(sig, lags = 4, horizon = 1, hidden_dim = 16,
                                  epochs = 40, seed = 2)
fst
c(last_train = max(fst$windows$train), first_val = min(fst$windows$val),
  first_test = min(fst$windows$test))
rbind(model = fst$test_metrics, naive = fst$baseline_metrics)
```

To bring your own data, build the graph with any of the constructors and
pass the array to `spatiotemporal_signal()`, which checks that the node
dimension matches.

## Memory based models: TGN

Snapshot models see the graph at a fixed resolution. A temporal graph
network (Rossi et al. 2020) works on the event stream directly. Every node
has a memory vector, a GRU updates it each time the node takes part in an
event, and the embedding used for prediction combines the memory with the
time since the last update and, optionally, the node's most recent
partners.

`train_tgn()` processes the training events in chronological batches. Each
batch is scored with the memory left by earlier batches only, and its own
events update memory at the start of the next batch, so no event ever
informs its own prediction. Validation and test continue the same memory
in time order without gradient updates.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
stream <- dataset_synthetic_temporal(num_events = 1500, seed = 1)
sp_t <- split_temporal(stream)
torch_manual_seed(1)
tgn <- tgn_model(stream$num_nodes, memory_dim = 32, time_dim = 8, embedding_dim = 32)
fit_tgn <- train_tgn(tgn, sp_t, epochs = 10, batch_size = 50, lr = 0.01, seed = 1)
fit_tgn$history
fit_tgn$test_metrics
```

Each event is scored against one random destination. The synthetic stream
repeats earlier pairs often, so memory and the learned node embeddings
(`node_embedding = TRUE`, the default) carry most of the signal.

The embedding can also look at each node's most recent partners. With
`embedding = "graph_attention"`, the variant the TGN paper found best,
multi head attention runs over the `num_neighbors` latest partners; keys
and values combine the partner's memory, the time since that interaction
and the event features, and the query comes from the node's own memory.
Only partners from earlier batches are visible, for the same reason as
above.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
torch_manual_seed(1)
tgn_att <- tgn_model(stream$num_nodes, memory_dim = 32, time_dim = 8, embedding_dim = 32,
                     embedding = "graph_attention", num_neighbors = 5, heads = 2)
fit_att <- train_tgn(tgn_att, sp_t, epochs = 10, batch_size = 50, lr = 0.01, seed = 1)
fit_att$test_metrics
```

The implementation has one embedding layer (one hop) and keeps the most
recent message per node; the paper's other message aggregators are not
included.

## The recurrent cell

`graph_gru_cell()` replaces the matrix products of a GRU with graph
convolutions, as in DCRNN and GConvGRU, so the hidden state of each node mixes
with its neighbors at every step. `temporal_gnn_model()` wraps it with an
output layer. Its output at step $s$ depends only on inputs up to step $s$;
the test suite checks this by changing later inputs and comparing.

```{r, eval = has_torch}
g <- sig$graph
tt <- graph_tensors(g)
torch_manual_seed(3)
m <- temporal_gnn_model(input_dim = 1, hidden_dim = 8, output_dim = 1)
xs <- lapply(1:5, function(s) torch_tensor(matrix(sig$features[s, , 1], ncol = 1)))
out <- m(xs, tt$edge_index)
length(out$outputs)
dim(out$outputs[[5]])
```
